extract:
Antonio Vivaldi was born on 4 March 1678 in Venice, then the capital of a still-glamorous if declining maritime republic, and died in Vienna on 28 July 1741. He is the central figure of the Italian Baroque concerto, and his active career spanned roughly from the first years of the eighteenth century to the late 1730s. Spotify catalogues his music under the italian baroque, baroque, early music and classical genres. His presence there consists largely of modern performances gathered into compilations such as Vivaldi: The Four Seasons (Remastered) and the many seasonal classical anthologies issued in 2026.

His first teacher was his father, Giovanni Battista Vivaldi, a barber turned professional violinist at St Mark's Basilica. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703. His red hair earned him the nickname il Prete Rosso, the Red Priest. He soon stopped saying Mass, citing a chronic chest ailment, and that same year began working at the Ospedale della Pietà, a Venetian institution for foundling girls whose all-female orchestra and choir became famous across Europe. Vivaldi served there as violin master and later in broader musical roles for much of his life. The Pietà gave him a resident ensemble on which to test an enormous output of concertos.

His reputation spread through printed collections published in Amsterdam by Estienne Roger. L'estro armonico, Op. 3 (1711), set out his concise three-movement form with bold ritornellos and virtuosic solo episodes, and it became one of the most influential publications of the age. La stravaganza, Op. 4, followed. Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione, Op. 8 (1725), contained the four violin concertos known as The Four Seasons, which are paired with descriptive sonnets and dedicated to the Bohemian Count Wenzel von Morzin. La cetra, Op. 9 (1727), was dedicated to Emperor Charles VI. Alongside these he wrote sacred works including the Gloria RV 589, the Stabat Mater and the oratorio Juditha triumphans (1716). He was also a prolific opera composer and impresario, beginning with Ottone in villa at Vicenza in 1713 and including Orlando furioso (1727) and Griselda (1735), whose libretto was revised by the young Carlo Goldoni.

His career extended well beyond Venice. From 1718 to 1720 he served Prince Philip of Hesse-Darmstadt at Mantua. His long association with the contralto Anna Girò, a frequent star of his operas, drew gossip. His most consequential admirer was Johann Sebastian Bach, who transcribed several of his concertos for keyboard. These include the Concerto for Four Harpsichords BWV 1065, adapted from Op. 3 No. 10. Through such arrangements, Vivaldi's ritornello procedures shaped the German concerto.

Taste in Venice moved on, and Vivaldi travelled to Vienna, apparently hoping for imperial patronage. Charles VI died soon after his arrival, and Vivaldi himself died there in poverty. For nearly two centuries he was remembered mainly through Bach. Revival came in the 1920s, when large manuscript collections were acquired by the National Library in Turin and studied by Alberto Gentili. Alfredo Casella followed with a Vivaldi week in Siena in 1939. Peter Ryom's catalogue later gave the works their standard RV numbers.

Postwar recordings made Vivaldi ubiquitous, notably I Musici's 1955 Four Seasons and Nigel Kennedy's 1989 version with the English Chamber Orchestra, which became one of the best-selling classical records ever. Period-instrument ensembles such as Il Giardino Armonico and Fabio Biondi's Europa Galante have since reshaped how he is heard. The Vivaldi Edition on the Naïve label has brought his neglected operas and sacred music back into circulation. Today The Four Seasons is among the most performed and recorded works in the classical repertoire, and its steady stream of reissues and compilations shows how far his music has travelled from the Pietà.
title: Antonio Vivaldi
